exam: A 32‑year‑old HIV patient presents with a chronic, painless ulcer on the leg; what is the most likely diagnosis and first test? — Sporotrichosis; do a KOH prep and culture on Sabouraud agar.
A 45‑year‑old farmer reports a painless, slowly enlarging nodule on the hand; what is the differential and treatment? — Chromoblastomycosis; treat with itraconazole or terbinafine.

A 28‑year‑old woman with fever, headache, neck stiffness; CSF shows 200 cells, low glucose; what is the most likely pathogen and treatment? — Cryptococcus neoformans; start amphotericin B + flucytosine.
You have a patient with a ring‑shaped, scaling rash on the scalp; what is the next step? — KOH prep to confirm dermatophyte infection.
A patient on fluconazole develops jaundice; what is the next step? — Stop fluconazole, check liver enzymes, consider switching to itraconazole.
You suspect a fungal pneumonia in a malnourished child; what is the empiric therapy? — Start amphotericin B if available, otherwise fluconazole; monitor renal function.
ai.title: Mycology Fundamentals
ai.subject: Microbiology & immunology
ai.summary: Fungi are chitin‑based organisms that can be yeasts, molds or mushrooms. In low‑resource East African settings, superficial, cutaneous, subcutaneous and systemic mycoses are common, often linked to HIV, TB or malnutrition. Clinicians must recognise clinical patterns, use simple diagnostics, and choose safe antifungals.

sections.p: Fungi are eukaryotic, chitin‑rich organisms that reproduce via spores. They are ubiquitous in soil, decaying matter and human skin. In resource‑limited hospitals, fungal infections often coexist with HIV, TB, malaria and malnutrition, complicating diagnosis and treatment.
Fungi lack chlorophyll and rely on external nutrients. Their cell wall contains β‑1,3‑glucan and chitin, making them resistant to many antibiotics but susceptible to azoles and polyenes.

Transmission is mainly via inhalation of airborne spores, skin contact with contaminated soil or water, or ingestion of contaminated food. Life cycle varies: yeasts reproduce by budding; molds by spore formation.

Superficial mycoses (tinea, candidiasis) affect skin, nails, mucosa. Subcutaneous mycoses (chromoblastomycosis, sporotrichosis) present as nodules or ulcers. Systemic mycoses (histoplasmosis, cryptococcosis) can be life‑threatening, especially in immunocompromised patients.

b: When microscopy is unavailable, use a simple wet mount with 10% KOH. If culture is delayed, empiric therapy may be started based on clinical suspicion.
sections.p: History of exposure, clinical morphology, and simple laboratory tests guide diagnosis. In low‑resource settings, microscopy, KOH prep, and culture are primary tools. Molecular tests are rarely available.

t.b: Detects fungal hyphae or yeast cells; a positive result confirms a fungal infection.
Highlights fungal structures; useful when KOH is unavailable.
Identifies species; growth within 7–14 days confirms diagnosis.
Detects cryptococcal capsule in CSF; a positive result indicates cryptococcal meningitis.
Rapid detection of cryptococcal antigen in serum or CSF; a positive result mandates treatment.

b: Avoid amphotericin B in patients with renal impairment; use lipid formulations if available.
sections.p: Treat the underlying cause first (e.g., antiretroviral therapy for HIV). Antifungals are chosen based on spectrum, toxicity and availability. Supportive care and monitoring are essential.

t.b: Treats candidiasis, cryptococcosis; a therapeutic response is seen within 1–2 weeks.
Effective for dermatophytes and subcutaneous mycoses; monitor liver function.
Reserved for severe systemic infections; monitor renal function and electrolytes.

b: Cryptococcal meningitis: treat with amphotericin B + flucytosine, then fluconazole.
sections.p: Remember that fungal infections often mimic bacterial or viral diseases. In HIV patients, cryptococcal meningitis presents with headache, fever, neck stiffness; a positive India ink or CrAg is diagnostic. For cutaneous lesions, a KOH prep can quickly confirm dermatophytes.

whenToSeekHelp: Severe headache with neck stiffness (possible meningitis), sudden visual loss (possible fungal optic neuropathy), respiratory distress from pulmonary fungal infection
